## Report: Olive Oil Consumption and Stroke Risk

The evidence generally supports your claim that consuming more olive oil reduces the risk of stroke, though some nuances exist.

**Meta-analyses and observational studies** consistently show an inverse association between olive oil consumption and stroke risk. A clinical nutrition study concluded that olive oil consumption is associated with a lower risk of both cardiovascular disease and stroke, with maximum benefits obtained at 20–30 g/day, and a potentially stronger protective effect for virgin olive oil. Similarly, a Frontiers meta-analysis found olive oil consumption inversely related to CVD and all-cause mortality, with benefits observed up to about 20 g/day.

A systematic literature review summarized that olive oil consumption significantly reduced the risk of CVD and stroke specifically, though the evidence for coronary heart disease alone was less consistent. This distinction is important—stroke appears to be one of the outcomes most clearly associated with olive oil's protective effect.

**Clinical trial evidence** comes from the landmark PREDIMED study, in which high-risk individuals assigned to a Mediterranean diet supplemented with extra-virgin olive oil experienced fewer major cardiovascular events (including stroke) compared to a control diet.

However, some caveats apply: epidemiological results have been described as inconsistent across studies, and researchers have noted that only future clinical trials can increase confidence and potentially lead to formal stroke prevention recommendations. The evidence is strongest within Mediterranean dietary patterns, and benefits may depend on the type of olive oil (virgin vs. refined) and the amount consumed.

- https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/nutrition/articles/10.3389/fnut.2022.1041203/full
- https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1800389
